Circle Of Similitude

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two circles and the blue circle through the places where their touching lines meet.
How to play: Drag the dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick Names or Hint to change what is shown, and press Reset picture to start again.
Look for the math

Move T anywhere on the blue circle and the two black circles keep the same ratio of distances, of tangent lengths and of apparent size. The picture is a theorem, not a puzzle with a win.

Where the touching lines meet

Two circles that lie apart have four common tangents. The two crossing ones meet at P between the centres, and the two outer ones meet at Q outside them. P and Q are the centres of the two homotheties that turn one circle into the other, with scale factors −R2/R1 and +R2/R1. The blue circle is drawn on PQ as its diameter. The logic test builds the tangents exactly as the old applet's bytecode does, intersects them, and gets the same P and Q for every tested pair of circles.

The blue circle keeps a distance ratio

P divides the centres internally and Q divides them externally in the ratio R1/R2, so the circle with diameter PQ is the circle of Apollonius for those two centres. Every point T on it satisfies d1/d2 = R1/R2. The test walks right round the blue circle for hundreds of generated pairs and finds the ratios equal to within a billionth. When the radii are equal there is no outer centre: Q runs off to infinity and the blue circle becomes the straight line midway between the centres — the page assumes different radii, but the same ratio rule still holds there.

Tangent lengths and equal angles

A tangent from T touches a circle at right angles to its radius, so the Pythagorean theorem gives d_i² = t_i² + R_i². Dividing the two copies by d1/d2 = R1/R2 leaves t1/t2 = R1/R2, exactly as the page claims. The right triangles with sides t_i, d_i and R_i are similar, so the angle between the two tangents from T, 2·arcsin(R_i/d_i), is the same for both circles. Tick Hint to see those equal angles. The test checked both formulas at thousands of points and they agreed at every one. One small change from the old code: it placed the blue circle's centre at the average of the x coordinates, with the first circle's y, which is only right when the centres are level; this page uses the true midpoint of PQ so the theorem holds after any drag.

Make the radii equal and watch Q disappear; then drag the two circles closer together until P leaves the picture and the common tangents vanish.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
